text: Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in Gaza in an Israeli strike, has posthumously won the prestigious Rory Peck prize for freelance video journalists, the organisers announced on Wednesday.

She shares the award with two of her colleagues from the Associated Press (AP), Abdel Kareem Hana and Jehad Alshrafi, “for their powerful coverage of the human cost of the war” in the Palestinian territory, the Rory Peck Trust said.
Dagga, who has a teenage son named Ghaith, was killed in August 2025 in an Israeli airstrike on a southern Gaza hospital, which claimed the lives of four other journalists.
The independent photographer and reporter had been working with the AP news agency since the beginning of the current conflict, triggered by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.

Dagga was renowned for her relentless reporting despite the personal losses she suffered throughout the war. She filmed the death of a protester who was shot during the 2018 Great March of Return in Gaza, when Israeli forces shot protesters marching towards the Gaza border fence, killing more than 220 people and wounding more than 9,200. She later discovered that the protester was her brother.
The war correspondent continued her work as a journalist during the war in Gaza over the last 22 months, working as a freelancer with the AP and Independent Arabia.
The AP’s executive editor, Julie Pace, said: “Journalists play an essential role in documenting events and informing the public, often at enormous personal risk.
“We honour Mariam and all journalists killed during this conflict and other conflicts – and remain committed to seeking answers about their deaths.”
French photographer Robin Tutenges was the recipient of the first Rory Peck award for photojournalism in recognition of his work on the conflict in Ethiopia’s northern Amhara region.

Sudanese freelance photographer and video journalist Ahmed Mohamed Abdalla, who works with Agence France-Presse, was shortlisted for the same award for his coverage of the fall of El Fasher to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Sudan’s civil war.
Abdalla was not allowed to attend the prize-giving ceremony in London as the UK government refused to grant him a visa.

In a recorded video message shared during the ceremony, he told of how the capital of the North Darfur region’s besieged inhabitants had to eat livestock feed to survive amid the daily deluge of missiles.
The prize has been awarded since 1995 in memory of Northern Irish video journalist Rory Peck, who was killed in Moscow in 1993, to celebrate the work of freelance video journalists.
